Last year, for example, Anthropic CEO Darius Amodei declared in an interview with </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4d7080d8-19a7-41b2-9c52-31667e57922a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Axios</span></a><span> that AI could wipe out half of entry-level white-collar jobs and drive overall unemployment as high as 20 percent within 1 to 5 years.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">More recently Amodei and OpenAI’s Sam Altman have tried to walk back their predictions of a “jobs apocalypse”. But why were they so willing to promote apocalyptic visions in the first place? The answer is money. They pushed the idea that they had a technology that would quickly and utterly transform the economy partly to dazzle Wall Street and secure financing, and partly to scare businesses into rushing into AI adoption for fear of being left behind.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Only belatedly did they realize that declaring that your technology will wreak devastation would lead to a public backlash, and that this backlash would be a serious problem. Indeed, it’s not just the general public that is lashing out against companies that use threats of an apocalypse as a marketing strategy. Even major corporations are saying that they’ve had enough. Satya Nadella, CEO of Microsoft, who has been noticeably unwilling to engage in AI fanaticism, recently told the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/b646ed83-c212-4ac8-ab17-edec0632900c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Wall Street Journal</span></a><span>:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #E8B500;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>You can’t say, hey, all white-collar jobs are gone and this could even be a weapon and we will use all the power to build data centers.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Second, many ordinary people view AI negatively </span><em>because they feel that it is being forced on them</em><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s true that many people are</span><s> </s><span>voluntarily using large language models for personal convenience or as a business productivity tool. But a significant part of AI use isn’t voluntary. This intense backlash is special.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And the backlash is already having major political consequences. But </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dfbd4a0f-3857-47bf-b3b5-806199c9d934?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>most of these efforts</span></a><span> have failed. Indeed, accepting AI money or being associated with tech in general is beginning to look politically </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/8ede5e4d-7fdb-4f2a-ab26-ce7ec2d1142a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>toxic</span></a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There’s a strong element of poetic justice in this turn of events. The AI industry deliberately made itself look menacing as a financial strategy, believing that the markets would reward the appearance of being “edgy.” In so doing, however, tech made itself highly unpopular. And even in an era in which money all too often buys power, public opinion matters.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">MUSICAL CODA</p><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/a5e11d3a-eb7a-49ce-9e23-18e5f5a9ec82?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="margin-bottom: 0;display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/w6iRNVwslM4" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>You’re currently a free subscriber to Paul Krugman. (Photo by </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/04fa9285-e269-4d60-8e80-ce263f5201d4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Grace Cary</span></a><span> via Getty Images)</span></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Not to be melodramatic, but I really believe the future of American democracy has been hanging in the balance the past few years. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">January 6, as it played out, was more farce than tragedy. But normally, a president who becomes unpopular and loses power is discredited within his own political party. The fact that Donald Trump was able to survive not only electoral defeat but the specter of a failed putsch was an ominous portent for the country. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">His ability to recapture the presidential nomination and then recapture the office itself is terrifying. And his second term has been a true “no guardrails” presidency. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s not that he’s suddenly a political superman who’s capable of anything; he remains quite constrained in his ability to accomplish all kinds of things. But the entire Republican Party has proven, time and again, that it will indulge Trump in essentially limitless levels of inappropriate conduct. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">We have flagrantly unfit leadership at the F.B.I. We’ve seen repeated purges of senior military commanders. Bill Pulte is not only abusing power at the Federal Housing Finance Agency in previously unthinkable ways, but that willingness to abuse power was essentially his qualification for promotion to serve as director of national intelligence. With his pardons, Trump has made clear that there will be no legal accountability for any crimes conducted by his political allies, and he’s had many appointees across a range of agencies make clear that the White House can and will order prosecutions and regulatory crackdowns on his enemies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The bad news for Americans’ well-being — but good news for the long-term future of the republic — is that Trump also massively fumbled the bag. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Rather than </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbc5f083-dc8b-48c0-9024-18f12fd68d11?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">following a template for political success</a><span> that would have allowed him to consolidate power, Trump has chosen overreach in almost every domain. And while his opportunistic promise to deliver a lower price level was never achievable, he was absolutely not forced to exacerbate inflation across multiple dimensions. These were voluntary blunders that have given the opposition a chance to beat him. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">And the opposition has really needed good luck, because despite widespread alarm about these threats, the entire progressive movement has done less than nothing to respond to them. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">While a hearty few souls have been organizing No Kings protests, the vast majority of activist energy has gone into a series of blue-on-blue primaries in safe districts, typically pitting an “establishment” politician whose views are already well to the left of the median voter against an insurgent whose views are identical on 90 percent of salient issues but who also says oligarchy and hates Israel. Even outside the circles of hardcore insurgents, the broad left-of-center media has displayed about 1,000 times more curiosity about what it takes to win primary elections in New York City than what it takes to beat Republicans in red-leaning areas.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But winning in red-leaning areas is what Democrats need to do. </p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up is-fully-subscribed" data-component-name="SubscribeWidget" style="margin: 0 0 1em;direction: ltr;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div Maine and Michigan, the decisive Senate race will be in Iowa or Ohio. With the Voting Rights Act gone, Republicans have been able to score a decisive advantage in gerrymandering and skew the House map heavily in favor of Trump, as the Senate already was. Democrats could easily win 52 percent of the vote nationally and see a Republican trifecta confirmed in place — except with Bill Cassidy and Mitch McConnell replaced by MAGA cultists. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The actual outlook, though, is better than that. Trump’s blundering and unpopularity, plus some good House and Senate recruiting, have put Democrats in a reasonable position to win. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Flipping both houses of Congress — and thus delivering a clear sign to American elites that this is not the time to surrender to authoritarianism — is not the most probable outcome, but it is on the table. To seize this chance, though, requires Trump opponents to focus on the thing that actually matters: not whether safe seat Democrats can be compelled to be even more uncompromising, but whether Democrats can win the key races. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The House is the states </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Democrats have long been favored to flip the House, and their lead in the generic ballot is so large that all the gerrymandering probably won’t make a difference. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It is worth flagging, though, that with Virginia Democrats’ effort to gerrymander thrown out by the state’s own court and a bunch of red states in the South unleashing aggressive new gerrymanders thanks to the Supreme Court killing the Voting Rights Act, the landscape is now genuinely quite skewed. It would be historically unusual for an unpopular incumbent to see a big recovery between now and Election Day. But if Republicans can depress the Democrats’ generic ballot edge from its current range of six or seven points to something like four, the G.O.P. could potentially win the House. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">The big issue here, though, is really 2028. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">There are basically two things that could happen between this November and the end of the next cycle. First, there are several blue states that are not currently gerrymander-maxed but whose own state rules made it impossible to redraw maps in the time between the Supreme Court’s ruling and Election Day 2026. Over the course of two more years, though, Illinois will almost certainly draw an additional blue seat. New York will likely draw one and perhaps two additional blue seats. Maryland will probably create one. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But to get to within striking distance of even, Democrats will also need action from Virginia, Colorado, Minnesota, and Washington state, all of which are less certain for various reasons, including the fact that their ability to act likely depends on the midterms. Slow Boring is working with collaborators on some future donation recommendations that will include strategically targeted state legislative races to try to help with this, so stay tuned!</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But another factor in play is Georgia. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Georgia did not join the red-state gerrymandering party, but it will have a new governor next year. If that governor is a Republican, Georgia will probably redraw. If the governor is a Democrat, it won’t. Democrats had a couple of strong contenders in the field, but the voters seem determined to go with former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms, who isn’t a terrible nominee but seems like clearly the worst option. Nonetheless, Trump is unpopular enough that Bottoms has a decent shot at winning. There are also secret stakes in this race where if Bottoms wins, Jon Ossoff can run for president or V.P. without giving away a seat.  </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The Senate paradox </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In the upper house, we have an odd situation in which Democrats seem to be in an unexpectedly strong position in some of the more challenging states, while a relatively easy race in Maine has become complicated and what ought to have been a layup in Michigan has turned into a clusterfuck. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">First the good. Mary Peltola is genuinely favored to win Alaska’s Senate seat. Without her, the whole landscape would look very different. Peltola’s life would’ve been a lot easier if she’d run for governor, but she chose to run for Senate. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">More than anyone else, she has “met the moment” in a real way, and Chuck Schumer talking her into it was a huge win. Every progressive NGO leader who ever gave her a hard time about anything while she was in the House should (but won’t) acknowledge that all their hopes and dreams hinge on her and make their apologies. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">In Iowa, by contrast, the best candidate (Rob Sand) did run for governor, but Democrats still ended up with a really good candidate in Josh Turek, a Paralympian who holds a red seat in the state legislature. Zach Wahls should have done the right thing and stood down rather than turning this into a pointlessly expensive primary, but the voters chose correctly and the Sand-Turek ticket should have some complementarities and mutually reinforcing strengths. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In Texas, what I’ve seen so far from James Talarico suggests he is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9f58d839-5c3f-4ba2-a14a-95f44a6773fc?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">taking the obligation to win seriously</a><span>. He’s seized the center ground on energy — touting “all of the above” in contrast to Trump’s efforts to kneecap renewables — and he’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ac14cbf-0a5a-48df-a357-65a6c7edbdc7?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">moved toward the center</a><span> on trans issues. He also appears to be collaborating with South Texas moderate Hispanics on a tactical level in a way that will hopefully unlock a good border message. This is a tough race that will cost a fortune and probably end in the election of crooked scumbag Ken Paxton, but the case for hope is real. </span></p><div class="subscribe-widget is-signed-up style="text-decoration: none;">Subscribed</span></a></div></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Ohio is the tough Senate race that I feel the most queasy about. Re-running Sherrod Brown makes some sense on paper but also strikes me as a little uninspired. Brown has moderated on cryptocurrency, which is good in the sense that it’s good to move to the center, but I think it’s a bit odd to treat his 2024 defeat as all about crypto spending. I was not a huge fan of his prior stance on this, but there are legitimate criticisms of the crypto industry and being anti-crypto was deeply consistent with Brown’s longtime populist persona. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">To me, what separates the Sherrod Brown who won repeatedly in Ohio from the one who lost in 2024 is that the earlier Brown was a moderate on energy, while the 2024 Brown seemed like a deer in the headlights on Biden-era immigration issues. He’s polling okay in this race and I hope he pulls it out, but I don’t feel confident in his campaign’s approach. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Much has already been written about Maine, and because I’ll be in Hancock County Maine (where Graham Platner is from) for most of the summer, I’ll probably end up covering this a lot. I just want to note here that Maine had a ton of ambitious, age-appropriate, well-vetted politicians, absolutely none of whom ran for Senate. That includes guys like Troy Jackson, a Bernie factionalist whose politics I don’t really agree with but who would have brought everything to the table that Platner fans like without some of the downsides. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This brings us to Michigan, a true fiasco. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Gretchen Whitmer would have cleared the field and easily won this race. But she pulled an anti-Peltola and is throwing a promising political career away for no clear reason. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Meanwhile, nothing this cycle has caused me more heartache than this primary. We have Abdul El-Sayed, a Bernie factionalist, running not in one of the D+infinity House seats that are the left’s specialty, but statewide in a swing state where even small underperformance could be deadly. The establishment kinda sorta but not really consolidated around Haley Stevens as their candidate but, while Stevens is a moderate, she’s actually a weak electoral performer. Mallory McMorrow, the third force in the race, has more political skills than Stevens, but those skills have mostly been deployed in ugly fighting with Stevens. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I have friends in both the McMorrow and Stevens camps, and unfortunately instead of working together to fix the party, the narcissism of small differences is creating a situation where El-Sayed will likely win the primary. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s a massively frustrating situation. Even without Whitmer in the race, there were better options like Kristen McDonald Rivet (one of the top electoral performers in the House) and Detroit Mayor Mike Duggan (who instead chose to run for governor as an independent and then drop out). Maine is the bluest state on the 2026 map, but it’s tough for Democrats because Susan Collins is tough. Michigan should have been easy, but instead it’s become very hard — a true blunder. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">Tactics versus strategy </h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think the tactical efforts of Democratic Party leaders have been a little under-appreciated. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Hakeem Jeffries has his people collaborating on actual House votes, winning discharge petitions, and doing a surprisingly good job of influencing the news agenda. With the exception of one House race in California (pour one out for Jasmeet Bains), he’s managed to keep the factional infighting firewalled from the important races. Redistricting ended up being fucked, but that’s not his fault. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Schumer, I think, is guilty of a legitimate brain fart in Maine, where there were many better places to park his hopes and dreams than in Janet Mills. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the Michigan situation, while a total nightmare, is not his fault. It’s not like he forgot to call Whitmer; she just chose to do the wrong thing. Iowa, Alaska, and Texas have all worked out quite well, and while I’m kind of gritting my teeth about Ohio, I do understand the play and I think this race is basically on Brown to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d500aca1-fb5b-4154-8937-a38d3639f0ed?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">read his old press coverage</a><span> and talk to some </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dde97107-5206-4060-af2b-0de7802beeee?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">steelworkers and people in the building trades about energy</a><span>. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But as a guy whose whole thing is complaining about Democrats, I really do want to emphasize that 80 percent of what’s keeping Democrats in the game here is Trump blundering. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To that you can add some strong </span><em>tactical</em><span> optimizations around candidate selection and messaging emphasis. My moderate-aligned friends who work in ads and testing are all really happy with the direction the party is going in. I am less pleased, because I think operatives tend to massively overrate paid media and direct-to-camera videos relative to strategic position-taking. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the national party has not made even token gestures at a rebrand. There’s nothing like the Republicans’ “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fc467b09-2515-46d6-91cd-ce4c9d8d5bd0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">young guns</a><span>” from 2010 or the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f9ce9c6b-c303-4d21-b347-9dbbe1767ba5?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">brand refresh</a><span> Democrats did in 2006. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I think Democrats think they’ve changed their pitch on immigration after the Biden fiasco, but I genuinely don’t understand what they think is different about it. They know that “affordability” is their best talking point against Trump, but that has meant rebranding ideas that were mostly developed in Obama’s second term rather than an actual renewed focus on interest rates and productivity. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’m trying to not be too whiny about this, because </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e02b48c1-a68b-4db1-a9b7-ebfe8d821bc2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #04b2a5;text-decoration: none;">Weber</a><span> specifically warns against the person who will “crumble when the world from his point of view is too stupid or too base for what he wants to offer.” The stakes are high, but there are real reasons for hope in these midterms and green shoots of the kinds of change that need to happen. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Democrats have under-reacted relative to what will maximize their odds in the midterms, and I really don’t want them to get complacent if they flip the House with two seats to spare. But there have been positive changes, and taking advantage of Trump’s screwups is a legitimate way to conduct politics. Relative to the disastrous situation the party was facing in the winter of 2024–25, things are looking up. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">It’s going to take a bunch of small things all going right to make me feel good about this November. boneheaded war with Iran</a><span>, blamed </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/448ada59-3836-478e-977c-0a73dfbdf574?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">algae in the Reflecting Pool</a><span> on nonexistent vandals, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c5693203-f5ff-4371-9319-16b6a77393cd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">tried to ban mail-in voting</a><span> by executive order, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/23a04276-9c58-481f-a43d-a491f002d877?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">refused to pass</a><span> a (very good) housing bill, issued an order calling for </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/17eafbeb-64d7-4074-9d16-ad78e59da86f?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">fewer childhood vaccines</a><span>, and so on. The man is a walking disaster, and a majority of the country </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fade6615-48d0-4d62-b74e-05c31d6ad536?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">recognizes it</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the movement that Trump started may end up being just as bad, or potentially even worse. After Trump leaves the scene, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/92a85771-d3f2-4538-8960-dc1d3535324d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">ideology will flow in to fill the gap</a><span> left by his personality cult. We already know more or less what that successor ideology will look like — intensely xenophobic, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/df24a840-5cb9-4b2d-aa7e-e3ad72d162f4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">obsessed with “Western civilization”</a><span>, virulently opposed to the EU (for supposedly betraying Western civilization) and favorably disposed toward Russia, conspiratorial, anti-science, anti-vaccine, and so on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both Trump and his movement are clearly a disaster and a dead end. That opens up space for Democrats to do one of two things. The first is to become more extremist, and hope that anti-Trump backlash and base turnout/mobilization will allow the Dems to squeak out narrow victories in 2028 or 2032. The second is to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/49c12001-8a14-4848-a185-4ffc6ef233ec?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">moderate and stand up staunchly in defense of liberalism</a><span>, attacking Trump’s corruption, economic policies, anti-democratic overreach, and general policy failure. This second approach would capture more swing voters, but would run the risk of inspiring tepid enthusiasm among the base.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">I see elements of both strategies emerging. The DSA may be winning mayoral races and some Congressional seats, but it’s extremely unlikely to have a Presidential nominee in 2028. Many mainstream Dems have been moderating on cultural issues. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But the fact that “go moderate or go extreme” is even a question at all right now for the Democrats is thanks to Trump. The backlash to Trump is exactly what has opened up the possibility for Dems to become more extreme and still win elections. Mamdani’s election in NYC was clearly intended as a middle finger to Trump, and it’s no coincidence that DSA membership surges when Trump is in the White House.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Faced with a threat like Trump, some people instinctively become pragmatic and decide to do whatever it takes to make the threat go away. But a lot of people just instinctively reach for whatever weapon they can hurl at the enemy, and the DSA is a weapon that’s convenient and seems sharp. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The next question, of course, is: What can break the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/81bbfbfe-9001-4c34-92ab-52d9a5028159?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">mutually reinforcing cycle</a><span> of radicalization? There are </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fb62dc4c-2c5d-4d95-a6d2-63613240f0b0?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">plenty of things</a><span> that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/69528570-70e0-403c-894e-7f91a88ed5b2?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">seem to work</a><span>, but the real message is that reasonable people have to stand up forcefully against the radicals. But it’s hard for moderate Dems to stand up to people like Mamdani right now, because voters are very mad at them. </span></p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The failures of mainstream progressivism make Democrats hungry for an alternative</h4><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In 2016, I wrote </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/46c0149c-93d5-4b4c-a074-f457389328e4?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">a post on my old blog</a><span> called “Trump happened because conservatism failed”. I argued that during the George Bush presidency, all of the pillars of the Reaganite conservatism that had dominated the GOP for three decades either achieved bad results or lost the culture wars outright:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #6B26FF;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">[I]n the past fifteen years, the three pillars of conservatism - economic, foreign-policy, and social conservatism - have all had huge, dramatic failures…</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Economic conservatism had two big failures. The first failure was when the Bush tax cuts failed to reverse income stagnation…</span><span>The second failure was when a lax regulatory climate </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d1a74c95-0e0c-4203-a3d2-d2a8b75135ab?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">appeared</a><span> to give rise to a financial crisis that devastated the job market…[T]he formula of "cut taxes and let businesses do as they see fit" is now pretty discredited…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Next, foreign policy conservatism. This failed during the George W. Bush administration, when Bush turned bellicose rhetoric into bellicose reality with the disastrous Iraq War. The Iraq War was a disaster because despite winning the war pretty handily and taking low casualties, we received no </span><em>gains</em><span>…</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Finally, social conservatism…Social conservatism promised to restore family values by promoting Christianity and resisting things like gay marriage…Secularism is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ded0ce5d-bce3-493b-aa02-88d8edced9c8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">rising rapidly</a><span>. Gay marriage </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/668af9c6-0028-4d0f-9d44-27e7d1723f73?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">enjoys wide support</a><span>, especially among the young. Americans have resoundingly rejected the values pushed on them by Christian conservatives in the 80s, 90s, and 00s.</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The situation with the Democrats isn’t exactly analogous. The mainstream liberalism of Bill Clinton and Barack Obama </span><em>didn’t </em><span>fail. The welfare state was expanded, and poverty fell. Mostly-universal health care was implemented, and the uninsured rate plummeted. Gay marriage and marijuana legalization gained wide acceptance. In fact, it’s exactly these successes that make me think that doubling down on the kind of liberalism I grew up with is </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/62707173-6f12-432f-921a-2b479c934db3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">still America’s best bet</a><span>.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But although the main policy thrusts of liberalism generally succeeded, the movement failed in other, more subtle ways. For one thing, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5326bce2-36e4-4905-a922-424f6294abf3?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">it failed to satisfy the dreams</a><span> of the burgeoning ranks of educated professionals that American universities were graduating. We produced more PhDs than we had teaching positions, more law grads than we had billable hours, more journalism school grads than we had desks at the New York Times. The downward mobility that many of America's educated “precariat” encountered probably pushed them toward socialism — a phenomenon known as a “revolution of rising expectations”. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Liberalism also didn’t have much of a foreign policy. Clinton and Obama both believed in “engagement” with China, which most people now believe was a disastrous failure. Democrats acceded to the Iraq War, at least for the first few years. Obama did nothing to stop Russia from seizing parts of Ukraine in 2014. Dems’ foreign policy seemed to consist of “just do nothing and hope for the best”. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Liberalism’s successes also failed to prevent the rise of Trump. For a while it seemed that the electoral victories of Bill Clinton and Barack Obama were pushing the GOP toward the center — George W. Bush was a “compassionate conservative” whose policies reduced homelessness and bolstered the welfare state, and Mitt Romney was a moderate big-government conservative in the tradition of Nelson Rockefeller. Even Trump won in 2016 in part by moderating on Social Security and gay marriage and adopting the labor movement’s position on free trade. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But Trump also represented a hard swerve to the right on racial issues — something most Dems had thought was settled. Dissatisfaction with liberalism’s failure to prevent the resurgence of 1920s-style racism drove lots of Democrats to 2010s-era wokeness and the activist movements of the “resistance” period.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Wokeness </span><em>itself </em><span>then failed in many respects. Police defunding was </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1ba81a98-492f-4680-a5e0-0e032c47c092?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">generally a disaster</a><span>, and was swiftly reversed in most cities. DEI and the trans movement alienated a lot of regular Americans. The </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7daecc92-e046-489b-b4b0-0ef5bcc6fc70?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">toxic online culture of Bluesky-style progressives</a><span> alienated a lot of elite Americans. The Biden administration’s decision to treat immigration like a cultural issue for the first three years of his presidency </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0448883f-72f0-4182-bc2e-4d20c3c21cf8?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">caused a backlash</a><span> and a flight to Trump in 2024. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In other words, Democrats succeeded at most of the things that liberals cared about in the 1980s and 1990s, but it wasn’t enough. They simultaneously pissed off their own base (by failing to stop Trump and fulfill young people’s dreams) </span><em>and </em><span>swing voters (by being too woke). This has given rise to a strange dynamic in which Democrats </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/70e8a18b-dad0-415f-8799-535ec233faae?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">struggle to win swing voters</a><span>, while Democratic primary voters just </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4f63df1-628f-4075-9bac-2d1dbf9a5547?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">keep on moving to the left</a><span>. Almost every demographic group in the nation has become more Republican in recent years:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px Singh</a></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">This is why the DSA in the Mamdani Era reminds me of MAGA. It’s an insurgent movement responding to a wave of discontent among the base, even though its extremist ideas will have a tough time winning over swing voters. To the extent it succeeds, it’ll do so more because of backlash than because its ideas are truly popular, but the movement will view even the narrowest of electoral victories as a sweeping mandate to reshape the country along truly radical lines. </p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">But what will those lines be? The DSA’s recent electoral victories — especially Mamdani’s mayorship — are beginning to make this a bit clearer. </p><h4 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.125em * 1);">The two Lefts are now one</h4><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The American left has always been deeply divided, even at its moments of greatest energy.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">³</span><span> In the 2010s, there was a deep and visible split between two factions: socialists and resistance progressives. Anyone who spent time in left-wing Facebook groups or left-leaning corners of old Twitter couldn’t help but notice the furious battles between “Berniebros” who wanted to focus more on the working class and economic issues, and more identitarian types who wanted to make race and gender the center of everything. The iconic moment of this battle was certainly when BLM protesters </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/39f67cf4-d8ec-491d-a5ab-0b2ca902c796?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">rushed the stage and yelled at Bernie Sanders</a><span>, calling his movement white supremacist.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This split actually goes back a long way. America’s “woke” progressive movement is a very old movement that </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/780daca5-3a4a-4b73-bfea-205031604d49?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">goes all the way back to abolitionism</a><span> — in a way, it’s America’s own original homegrown left. Class-focused socialism, in contrast, is largely a European transplant, and has generally struggled to find a foothold in a nation too focused on racial divides to develop Europe-style class consciousness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But as I always say, these two strains of the American left are a bit like </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2019e690-9378-4ac6-8b15-ce3898a239d1?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the fundamental forces of nature</a><span> — at very high energies, they become the same thing. Tons of Bernie fans marched in the Floyd protests in 2020, and the DSA itself — as you can see from Avila Chevalier’s social media posts — is extremely “woke” on racial issues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The thing that really pumped energy into the new Mamdanian left wasn’t Trump — it was Palestine. The Palestine protests </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a1729b63-2cab-49a8-9ea5-e51f221b48ca?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">failed to capture the hearts of the nation</a><span> like BLM did in 2020, but they united a new generation of leftist activists behind a single passionate cause.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Palestine didn’t just inspire the imaginations of leftist Zoomers — it gave the DSA and the socialist movement an issue that the Democratic establishment couldn’t triangulate. Remember that Biden actually implemented many of the things that Bernie Sanders and his movement wanted — he forgave huge amounts of student loans, passed something very much like a Green New Deal, and threw more government money at health care.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But this only made the socialists hate Biden more. The socialist movement has always been an intensely factional project — actual policies aren’t as important as whose gang is in charge.</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">⁴</span><span> Bernie Sanders always emphasized </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1eedde2b-3235-4580-9737-795c47409b39?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">the need to overthrow the Democratic establishment</a><span>, and he always hired people from within the socialist movement, even when this required hiring grossly incompetent and somewhat wacky people. For factionalists obsessed with taking over the Democratic party, Biden’s adoption of many of Bernie’s core issues was anathema, precisely because it made such a takeover less likely. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Palestine was an issue that the Democratic establishment couldn’t triangulate. The Dems are less pro-Israel than the GOP — Obama’s Iran deal demonstrates that — but actually throwing a U.S. ally under the bus was a bridge too far for the institutional descendants of Bill Clinton, LBJ, JFK, and FDR. The anti-Israel movement’s fringe of antisemitism also probably scared Jewish members of the Democratic establishment into not supporting the Palestine cause. The sheer moral repugnance of the October 7th attacks — which socialists like Avila Chevalier have been willing to ignore or even endorse — also helped make it a perfect wedge issue.</p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Trump may have enabled the DSA to widen its support base, but it’s </span><em>Palestine</em><span>, not opposition to Trump, that provides the animating spark for the leftist resurgence. It’s a culture war wedge issue and a litmus test. It’s something that leftist leaders can speak passionately about, in uncompromising terms that energize their base and signal to swing voters that they have deep-seated values. It gives the foot soldiers an enemy to hate — the villainous AIPAC, whose money the DSA sees as its archnemesis. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Detractors (including myself) have called the Palestine movement an “omnicause”, noting how it muscled other leftist hobbyhorses like climate change and health care out of the discourse. But paradoxically, this will probably make DSA leaders more </span><em>pragmatic </em><span>in power — at least, unless and until they take the Presidency. Would the DSA implement Venezuela-style socialism if they controlled the Presidency and both houses of Congress? Probably, yes. But that stuff isn’t a big deal right now, because what matters is winning elections. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Just look at Mamdani. He </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/816b592e-88ec-45d5-ae36-19c85be3e04c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">came into office promising</a><span> government-run grocery stores, free buses, a rent freeze, universal child care, etc. In office, he has </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/5afff721-fe14-4a1d-b33a-17a5acdca20d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">governed like a moderate</a><span>, abandoning most of his expensive proposals and doing some surprisingly pragmatic things like supporting small businesses. He’s free to do this because A) American socialism is ideologically plastic, and B) his support for Palestine will never waver. Avila Chevalier will be the same — she’ll </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a211b166-e1ab-4454-a1f3-4989d56beb02?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">call for universal job guarantees and universal basic income and whatever</a><span>, but in the end she’ll probably just vote with the Democrats until it comes to anything involving Palestine. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The DSA’s all-in support for Palestine has also elevated the importance of Islam in the progressive movement. Note that Darializa Avila Chevalier </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9943643c-c249-430d-b64f-9411e0b77aed?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">converted to Islam</a><span> during the Palestine protests. Mamdani is not a strictly religious Muslim, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c59ee936-4a03-4a48-a246-91f78b2c5fcd?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">speaks about how </a><span>his Islamic background gave him respect for social justice, anti-imperialism, and so on. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is a synthesis that some people call “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/88da0241-9979-4355-b3b5-f0c99201db3a?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">Islamo-leftism</a><span>”.  The idea is not that leftism is a front for Islamic interests</span><span class="footnote-anchor-email" data-component-name="FootnoteAnchorToDOMStatic" style="font-size: 20px;">⁵</span><span> — Islamo-leftism has no interest in sharia law. Nor is this the Iranian Revolution of 1979, where a leftist vanguard unwittingly acted as an advance wave for Islamists who eventually took over. In fact, it’s almost the opposite. It’s the idea that Islam is being used to invigorate, inspire, and help further the </span><em>leftist </em><span>cause. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There are several advantages to this approach. First, it allows attacks on socialists to be portrayed as Islamophobic, taking advantage of Americans’ natural impulse to protect minority identities from discrimination and bigotry. Second, it </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4498d7c3-6f8c-4491-b067-b718e813cf13?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">helps the socialist movement leverage</a><span> the massive</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c2be1674-1f15-4f32-ad99-9bfb1bb0f8c6?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;"> wave of talent</a><span> from high-skilled Muslim immigration (Mamdani being a prime example). Third, it imbues the American Left with “anti-imperialist” bona fides, since European countries colonized many Muslim countries back in the age of colonialism. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It would be way too much to claim, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/99bfdf2b-6b76-4b97-b4f6-7f9f883aae3d?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">some conservatives do</a><span>, that the rise of the DSA signals a shift away from focusing on Black people to focusing on Muslims. But it will probably involve a modest recalibration. Muslim progressives — children of high-skilled immigrants like Mamdani, and educated converts like Avila Chevalier — will probably win some power in the Democratic party at the expense of older Black Christian and (especially) Jewish leaders. Islamophobia will certainly be elevated — and antisemitism downgraded — in the pantheon of social ills that progressives promise to combat. This might not appeal to working-class people of color, but it will definitely appeal to the educated, mostly-White urban progressives who </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/844cdfc6-ebc5-4d76-998f-1aaf2584e933?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">powered Avila Chevalier’s election</a><span> and who increasingly form the core support base of the Democratic Party. </span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So this is what I think we can look forward to in Democratic party politics over the next few years. DSA types will promise big socialist projects that never get implemented, while lambasting the Democratic establishment on Palestine to create a wedge issue, and taking advantage of the anti-Trump backlash to win electoral victories. They will govern surprisingly pragmatically, leading some </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2766e7ed-9e04-4aab-b4a6-ea4d60d3573e?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">admiring progressives</a><span> from outside their movement to think of them as “</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4785b0fc-eab7-4d58-9e76-da8c81ba8a4c?j=eyJ1IjoiNHd4eHhhIn0.THiPlOhlJVrM95bfyrnJXrugnT66pFY3JaSTi-_WlgE" style="color: #6b26ff;text-decoration: none;">sewer socialists</a><span>” who get things done. And to the extent that they gain control over foreign policy, they will be more sympathetic to Russia and China, and hostile to Ukraine and Taiwan. They’ll be smarter than MAGA — these are Democrats we’re talking about, after all — but will retain similarly transformative goals.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;">Whether their rise continues, of course, depends on a lot of things — whether Trump’s movement flames out, whether America’s mainstream liberals can reinvigorate their own movement, and so on. But for now, I think this is the equilibrium we’re heading towards.</p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr style="margin: 32px 0;padding: 0;height: 1px;background:
